Settled event contracts book in two places: the ticket that bought them takes a negative entry for what it cost, which is a cost leg and not a loss, and the settlement itself books separately — at 1 where it paid, at 0 where it expired worthless. buckets.note: Reopened in August for a systematic build, graded on returns again from Sep 20 and reviewed at year end. Counted from booked settlements, which lag the trade by up to a week, so the most recent weeks are always incomplete here.

insights: Loss asymmetry is still the leak. The average loser runs 1.5× the average winner, so a 59.9% hit rate finishes behind. The targets are being picked correctly; the losses are being let off the leash.

The engine is real: covered-call premium takes 78% of its closes at a 3.8 profit factor across 182 closes. That is the business, and everything else is management around it. It was switched off for two weeks at the start of September and switched back on in the week of Sep 7, and in the week of Sep 14 it completed a full turn: KEEL's calls were assigned at a strike above what the shares cost. The gap cost nothing visible, which is precisely why it is easy to let happen again.

The forecast sleeve reopened on Aug 24 to gather data for a systematic strategy under construction, and it is graded on what it returns again from Sep 20, back to the week it reopened. Scored on booked settlements it has been quietly positive and very small: about +0.15% of net asset value in the week of Aug 24, +0.12% in the week of Aug 31, +0.18% in the week of Sep 7, with the week of Sep 14 still unbooked. That is roughly half a point of net asset value across a month in which it staked two to three per cent of the book at a time, most of it in JPUSD — a root the strategy bans on 96 settled events at minus four cents a contract. Winning small on a banned root is the trap the ban exists for. The sleeve is monitored on size and on which roots it touches, it now trades a minimum of 100 contracts an action, and it is reviewed at year end on what it has actually produced.

Share legs run a 0.34 profit factor across 35 closes, nearly all of it traceable to two names held past their stops. The per-name cap is scar tissue from this line, and it has now held for seven consecutive weeks — the longest clean run in the record.

The ledger moves on the back office's schedule, not the market's. NU's August assignment reached the trade feed a week after the fact and NIQ's followed the same path; KEEL's has not landed yet. Event contracts are the sharpest case: a settled contract books its cost against the ticket that bought it and its payout as a separate settlement row, and those rows can lag by a week — as of Sep 20 not one of the 700 contracts settled in the week of Sep 14 had booked either leg. Read a fresh week of event trades as incomplete rather than as a loss. Two cards on this site were written the other way and have been corrected.

concepts.h: What we hold to be true
ul: Edge is process, not prediction.
Harvest premium. Do not chase direction.
Size is the risk lever. The entry is not.
Define the loss before taking the position.
Most of the tape is noise. Separating it is the work.

p: A handful of durable ideas carry the book: asymmetry — small, defined risk against convex payoff; premium taken from names the crowd overpays to insure; and the discipline to accept that sizing, not selection, is where most books are killed.
Looking like a mad hatter today and being right over the long run is the intended outcome, provided the fundamentals underwrite the view.

The watchlist runs across financials, defense, technology, and petrochemicals. Themes under current interest: artificial intelligence, robotics, satellite communications, credit and insurance, and founder-led firms — with several more held off the page.

discipline.h: The largest position is the trader
p: The principal risk to this book is not the tape — it is the person marking it. Conviction that turns into size. A winner that talks you into a bigger bet. A loser held because selling it makes the loss real. Temperament is the position that has cost the most, and the control framework exists to constrain it rather than to trust it.

ul: Concentration — no more than 20% of NAV in any single name. A hard limit, not a target.
Liquidity — a 10% cash floor at all times. Dry powder is a position, and it is the one that buys the dislocation.
Loss control — stops marked before the order goes in, and honored. No averaging down a broken thesis.
Thesis — every position carries one before it is sized. The typical trade runs entry, target, exit; investments are held outright and not collateralized.

p: Positions are marked daily; the limits are tested every Friday in the after-action. Three dials — concentration, cash floor, event exposure — each passed or breached, and the week is graded on discipline rather than on P&L alone. A green week with a breached limit still grades badly. Breaches are not quietly closed out: cash ran to 0.7% against a 10% floor in the week to Aug 14, and that sits in the permanent record next to the +3.2%.

One oversized position gave back months of grinding. The per-name limit, the cash floor, and the stop discipline are scar tissue — written down so the lesson does not get paid for twice. Limits are set when the book is calm and enforced when it is not. That is the whole reason they are written down at all.

This is a single-manager book. There is no independent risk function here and no second line of defence, and the framework does not pretend otherwise. It compensates the only way it can: the limits are mechanical, the tests are identical every week, and the results are published whether or not they flatter. Self-reporting is worth nothing unless the failures appear too.

Pareidolia is the mind's tendency to see meaningful patterns — faces — in random noise. The idea started as a university capstone and was rebuilt for markets: read the world like an operator, keep the fundamentals in hand, and accept looking like a mad hatter today if the long arc proves the read.
No house view and no consensus to hide behind. We form the read ourselves, size it deliberately, and let a written framework — not the mood of the tape — hold the book.

Pareidolia was built from the ground up, on partner capital and no outside scaffolding. The intent was never to stay small — it is to compound a durable, inspectable process into something far larger, one disciplined decision at a time.
A BBA in Finance from the University of Houston, class of 2023. Investing since January 2020, trading since January 2024.
It started strictly in securities — stocks, nothing else. I got bored and frustrated with that alone, and confused by the financial dogma handed down as fact, so trading was the logical next step.

It mutated out of light margin use. It started with buying weekly out-of-the-money calls and evolved with every trade made and lost. The toolkit now: cash-secured puts, covered calls, straddles and strangles, and LEAPS calls.
ul: Quirks. Brokers getting in the way, Reg T margin calls, wash sales, and getting scalped on illiquid names.

Risk. Tail events and illiquidity. Scaling up can set off several accidental wash sales, and opinions have to stay adaptive. The largest single-trade loss is withheld here, like every dollar figure on this site.
